Insufficient width means each layer's representation is a bottleneck. Either way, the learned function is too simple relative to the data's complexity. Optimization failure — poor learning rate (too high causes divergence, too low causes stagnation), bad initialization, or vanishing gradients in deep networks can prevent the model from converging even if it theoretically has enough capacity. sectionB_deep_neural_networks_q10: A protein's function is determined not by its amino acid sequence alone, but by the three-dimensional shape that sequence folds into. A chain of hundreds of amino acids folds into a precise, stable geometry in milliseconds inside a cell — driven by physical and chemical forces. Understanding that shape is essential for knowing what the protein does, how it malfunctions in disease, and how a drug might bind to it.Determining protein structure experimentally — through X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, or NMR spectroscopy — can take years of work and millions of dollars per protein. As of 2020, only roughly 170,000 structures had been solved experimentally, despite there being hundreds of millions of known sequences. The gap between known sequences and known structures is the central bottleneck in structural biology. AlphaFold 2 takes a raw amino acid sequence as input and outputs the full three-dimensional atomic coordinates of the folded protein — predicting where every atom sits in space, with accuracy competitive with experimental methods. The core of AlphaFold 2 is the Evoformer block, a novel architecture that maintains two coupled representations simultaneously: a per-residue representation and a pairwise representation encoding the relationship between every pair of residues. These two representations update each other iteratively through attention operations — the pairwise representation informs how residues attend to each other, and the residue-level updates feed back into the pairwise representation. After dozens of these coupled update cycles, the pairwise representation encodes rich geometric constraints about which residues are near each other in 3D space.

sectionB_linear_regression_q10: The standard loss function minimized during linear regression training is the Mean Squared Error (MSE), which calculates the average of the squared differences between predicted and actual values. This function is preferred because it is differentiable, allowing for efficient optimization via gradient descent, and it penalizes larger errors more heavily than smaller ones. When evaluating model fit, researchers often examine residuals plotted against fitted values; if this plot reveals a parabolic or U-shaped pattern, it indicates that the linearity assumption has been violated and the relationship between variables is likely non-linear. ​In Multiple Linear Regression, it is critical to check for multicollinearity, which occurs when independent variables are highly correlated. This issue inflates the standard errors of the coefficients, making the model unstable and results difficult to interpret; the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) is the most common measure used to detect it. When deciding between a high-degree polynomial and a simple linear model, there is a fundamental trade-off between bias and variance. While a high-degree polynomial may achieve a perfect fit on training data, it often overfits by capturing noise, whereas a simple linear model typically generalizes better to future predictions by capturing the underlying signal. ​If the relationship between the independent variable X and dependent variable Y is exponential, a logarithmic transformation is proposed. By applying a natural log to Y, the exponential curve is linearized, satisfying the OLS assumptions of linearity and homoscedasticity. In the broader context of machine learning, recommendation systems address similar data challenges. Content-based filtering suggests items by analyzing item features and tags, whereas collaborative filtering relies on user-item interactions. Both methods often struggle with the "cold start problem," which occurs when the system lacks sufficient historical data to provide accurate recommendations for new users or items.

sectionB_linear_regression_q9: The short answer is that a simple linear model (or a low-degree polynomial) almost always generalizes better to future, unseen data.  In machine learning and statistics, this scenario perfectly highlights the Bias-Variance Tradeoff, the tension between a model being too simple to capture the underlying pattern (underfitting) and a model being so complex that it memorizes the random noise in the data (overfitting).  A high-degree polynomial has immense flexibility. If you have 20 data points, a 19th-degree polynomial can snake its way through every single point, achieving a perfect training error of zero. But real-world data is composed of two things: the true underlying pattern (signal) and random fluctuations or measurement errors (noise). A highly complex model is so desperate to connect the dots that it learns the noise as if it were a permanent rule. As a result, when you introduce new data for future prediction, the model's wild, highly mathematical oscillations will completely miss the new points. This is called high variance.  A simple linear model is rigid. It cannot physically bend to touch every single training point, meaning it will always have some error on your training set (known as bias). Because it cannot bend, it is forced to ignore the random noise. It cuts right through the middle of the data, capturing the true, broad underlying trend. So when new data points arrive, they will likely fall close to that broad trend line. The model hasn't learned the quirks of the training data, so it remains stable and reliable.
sectionB_linear_regression_q10: The standard approach is to apply a logarithmic transformation to the dependent variable (Y). Instead of training your linear regression model to predict Y, you train it to predict the natural logarithm of Y, which is written as ln(Y). If we apply the natural logarithm to both sides of that exponential equation, we can use basic log rules to "unbend" the curve.  Linear regression fundamentally assumes the relationship between features and the target is linear, and this transformation forces it to meet this assumption. Additionally, in raw exponential data, the errors (residuals) get larger as X gets larger (violating the assumption of homoscedasticity, or constant variance). Taking the log stabilizes this variance. Also, it allows you to use the simple, fast, and highly interpretable mechanics of linear regression on non-linear data. To get your final prediction back in the original scale, you simply exponentiate the model's output.
sectionB_logistic_regression_q9: In almost all real-world scenarios for machine failure prediction, you should prioritize Recall over Precision.    If your model misses a failure, the machine breaks down unexpectedly during production. This leads to catastrophic downtime, entire assembly lines halting, expensive emergency part replacements, delayed shipments, and potential safety hazards for workers. But, if your model triggers a false alarm, a maintenance worker has to walk over, inspect the machine, and perhaps run a diagnostic test. They realize it's fine and go back to work. The cost is minimal. You would only prioritize Precision if the cost of checking the machine is worse than the machine breaking.
sectionB_logistic_regression_q10: 1. The Standard Approach: Softmax Regression If you have 3 classes, you calculate 3 separate raw scores for a given data point—one for each class. To turn these competing scores into a clean set of probabilities, you replace the Sigmoid function with the Softmax function.  2. The Alternative: One-vs-Rest (OvR) If you are strictly using algorithms that can only perform binary classification, you can use the One-vs-Rest (also called One-vs-All) strategy.  Instead of building one model, you build three separate binary models: Model 1: Is it Class A, or is it [Class B or C]? Model 2: Is it Class B, or is it [Class A or C]? Model 3: Is it Class C, or is it [Class A or B]?  When a new data point arrives, you run it through all three models. Each model gives you a confidence score or probability that the item belongs to its specific class. You simply look at the three outputs and declare the winner based on whichever model was the most confident.

Fuzzy Control: Operates on continuous degrees of membership (values in [0, 1]). sectionB_word_embedding_q10: Application: Intent Classification in Conversational AI (Virtual Assistants).  How it improves performance: It solves the "Zero Lexical Overlap" problem. Word embeddings, however, mathematically map "phone" near "mobile" and "broken" near "shattered" in the vector space. sectionB_recommender_system_q10: I propose a Weighted Hybrid Architecture  to solve the new item cold-start problem.  Phase 1 (Initial Release): When a new item is added, it lacks user interaction data, making Collaborative Filtering (CF) fail. The system will rely heavily  on Content-Based Filtering. It analyzes the new item's metadata (e.g., keywords, categories, descriptions) and recommends it to users who have historically liked similar features.  Phase 2 (Data Accumulation): As the new item begins receiving clicks and ratings from those initial recommendations, the system dynamically adjusts its weights. It gradually incorporates Collaborative Filtering (User-User or Item-Item) to leverage actual community behavior and discover deeper latent relationships, seamlessly transitioning from a pure content-based approach to a fully hybrid model.
